content: The Minister for Health and Children in Ireland is the senior official within the Department of Health and Children, tasked with overseeing healthcare services and related policies in the Republic of Ireland. The current Minister for Health and Children is Mary Harney, TD. She is supported by three Ministers of State: Brendan Smith, TD, who focuses on children’s issues; Máire Hoctor, TD, who addresses matters concerning older people; and Jimmy Devins, TD, who is responsible for disability issues and mental health. Historically, healthcare responsibilities were part of the portfolio of the Minister for Local Government and Public Health until January 22, 1947. On that date, the position of Minister for Health was established, granting full authority over healthcare policy in Ireland. In some instances, the health portfolio was combined with the social welfare portfolio, and the officeholder was then referred to as the Minister for Health and Social Welfare. However, in recent decades, particularly since Michael Noonan’s tenure from 1994 to 1997, the role of Minister for Health has been perceived as a challenging and often undesirable position within the government. This perception stems from the association of the role with numerous high-profile scandals, many of which involved medical negligence. Examples include the Hepatitis C scandal, the unauthorized retention of baby organs without parental consent, and the controversies surrounding Dr. Michael Neary in Drogheda. These incidents have often placed the Minister and the Department under intense public scrutiny. In addition to managing these crises, the Minister must address logistical challenges unique to the healthcare sector, such as strikes, resource shortages, and long waiting times in clinics and hospitals across the country. The Minister’s responsibilities encompass the development and evaluation of policies for the health services. The Department of Health and Children is organized into several key policy areas, each with specific duties: 1. Child Care: This includes child care legislation and oversight of the National Children’s Office. 2. Continuing Care: This area focuses on services for homeless adults, individuals with disabilities, the elderly, and those requiring palliative care. 3. Finance: Responsibilities include health insurance, hospital planning, and public-private partnerships. 4. Personnel Management and Development: This involves nursing policy and the management and development of healthcare personnel. 5. Primary Care: This includes community health services such as child health, dental care, AIDS prevention, and reproductive health, as well as general medical services. 6. Secondary Care: This area covers blood policy and hospital services. 7. Strategic Policy and Corporate Services: This includes corporate services, health promotion, and health strategy legislation. The office of the Minister for Health has evolved over time. From 1924 to 1947, healthcare was managed under the title of Minister for Local Government and Public Health. From 1947 to 1997, the position was known as the Minister for Health. Since 1997, the title has been Minister for Health and Children. In some cases, Ministers who simultaneously held the Health and Social Welfare portfolios are marked with an asterisk in historical records. The Department of Health has often been referred to as a challenging environment for its Ministers. For instance, Brian Cowen famously likened the Department to Angola, referencing the metaphorical landmines that exist within its jurisdiction.
